acceptedAnswer.text: Operators in Java are special symbols or keywords that perform operations on one or more operands and produce a result. Java provides a rich set of operators grouped into 8 categories: Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), Relational (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=), Logical (&&, ||, !), Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~), Shift (<<, >>, >>>), Assignment (=, +=, -=, etc.), Unary (++, --, +, -, !), and Ternary (?:). Operators are the building blocks of all expressions in Java — from simple calculations to complex conditional logic.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: == compares references (memory addresses) for objects and values for primitives. .equals() compares the actual content/value of objects. For primitives (int, char, etc.), always use ==. For objects like String, Integer, and custom classes, always use .equals() for content comparison. Example: String a = new String('hello'); String b = new String('hello'); a == b is false (different objects), but a.equals(b) is true (same content). The String pool can make == work for string literals, but this is an implementation detail — never rely on it.

mainEntity.name: What is short-circuit evaluation in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Short-circuit evaluation means Java stops evaluating a logical expression as soon as the result is determined. For && (AND): if the left operand is false, the right operand is never evaluated (false AND anything = false). For || (OR): if the left operand is true, the right operand is never evaluated (true OR anything = true). This is important for null checks: 'if (obj != null && obj.getValue() > 0)' — if obj is null, obj.getValue() is never called, preventing NullPointerException. The non-short-circuit operators & and | always evaluate both sides.

mainEntity.name: What is operator precedence in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Operator precedence determines the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression when multiple operators appear. Higher-precedence operators are evaluated first. From highest to lowest (simplified): postfix (x++), unary (-x, !x), multiplicative (*, /, %), additive (+, -), shift (<<, >>), relational (<, >, instanceof), equality (==, !=), bitwise AND (&), bitwise XOR (^), bitwise OR (|), logical AND (&&), logical OR (||), ternary (?:), assignment (=, +=, etc.). When in doubt, use parentheses to make precedence explicit and improve readability.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between prefix and postfix increment operators?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prefix (++x): increments the value FIRST, then returns the new (incremented) value. Postfix (x++): returns the current (original) value FIRST, then increments. Example: int x = 5; int a = ++x; — a = 6, x = 6 (prefix). int y = 5; int b = y++; — b = 5, y = 6 (postfix). When used as a standalone statement (not inside an expression), both are equivalent. The difference only matters when the expression value is used — inside assignments, method calls, or complex expressions.

articleHeader.title: Java Operators — Types, Syntax, Examples & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java Operators — arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment, unary, ternary, instanceof, operator precedence, short-circuit evaluation, anti-patterns, and real-world production code examples.

blocks.text: Operators are special symbols or keywords in Java that perform operations on one or more operands (values or variables) and produce a result. Every expression in Java — from simple arithmetic to complex conditional logic — is built using operators. For example, in int sum = a + b, the + is the operator and a, b are operands.

Java provides a rich set of operators organized into 8 major categories. Understanding operators deeply is foundational — they appear in every Java program and are frequently tested in interviews. Mastering operator precedence, short-circuit evaluation, and the subtle differences between similar operators (like == vs .equals(), or & vs &&) separates good Java developers from great ones.

Operators can be classified by the number of operands they work on: Unary operators work on one operand (++x), Binary operators work on two operands (a + b), and the Ternary operator works on three operands (condition ? val1 : val2). Java is the only operator that is ternary.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Operators at a Glance
blocks.text: Java supports 8 categories of operators: (1) Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %) — mathematical calculations. (2) Relational/Comparison (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=) — compare values, return boolean. (3) Logical (&&, ||, !) — combine boolean expressions. (4) Assignment (=, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, etc.) — assign values to variables. (5) Unary (++, --, +, -, !) — operate on a single operand. (6) Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~) — operate on individual bits. (7) Shift (<<, >>, >>>) — shift bits left or right. (8) Ternary (?:) — compact if-else in a single expression. Additionally, instanceof checks object type.

Java operators are grouped by the type of operation they perform. Each category has distinct rules, use cases, and pitfalls. The table below gives a quick overview before we dive into each one in detail.

Arithmetic operators perform standard mathematical operations. Java supports five arithmetic operators: addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/), and modulus (%). The + operator also works as string concatenation when used with String operands — this is one of the most common sources of subtle bugs in Java.

items.title: Integer Division vs Float Division
items.text: In Java, dividing two integers always produces an integer result (truncates toward zero, not rounded). 7 / 2 = 3, not 3.5. To get a decimal result, at least one operand must be a float or double: 7.0 / 2 = 3.5, or (double) 7 / 2 = 3.5. This is the #1 arithmetic bug in beginner Java code — always cast to double when decimal precision is needed.

items.title: Modulus (%) Operator
items.text: The modulus operator returns the remainder of division. 10 % 3 = 1, 15 % 5 = 0. Works with floating-point numbers too: 10.5 % 3.2 = 0.9 (approx). With negative numbers, the result takes the sign of the dividend (left operand): -7 % 3 = -1. Common uses: checking even/odd (n % 2 == 0), cycling through indexes (index % arrayLength), time calculations (seconds % 60).

items.title: String Concatenation with +
items.text: When + involves a String operand, it performs concatenation instead of addition. 'Hello' + ' World' = 'Hello World'. 'Value: ' + 5 = 'Value: 5'. But: 1 + 2 + ' apples' = '3 apples' (left-to-right: 1+2=3, then 3+' apples'). Vs: 'apples: ' + 1 + 2 = 'apples: 12' (String+int concatenates). Use parentheses to control evaluation order.

blocks.label: ArithmeticOperators.java
lines: System.out.println(a + b + " is sum");  // '19 is sum' — adds first (no String left)
// int x = 5 / 0;     // ❌ Throws ArithmeticException: / by zero
double y = 5.0 / 0;   // ✅ Returns Infinity (no exception for double)
double z = 0.0 / 0;   // ✅ Returns NaN (Not a Number)

blocks.text: Relational operators compare two values and always return a boolean result (true or false). They are the foundation of all conditional logic in Java — used in if, while, for, and ternary expressions. Java provides six relational operators: ==, !=, >, <, >=, and <=.

blocks.label: RelationalOperators.java
lines: System.out.println(x != y);  // true  — not equal to
System.out.println(x >= 10); // true  — greater than or equal
System.out.println(x <= 10); // true  — less than or equal
// ⚠️ CRITICAL: == on objects compares REFERENCES, not content
// ⚠️ String pool: literals may share reference — don't rely on this
System.out.println(s3 == s4);  // true (pool) — but NEVER use == for Strings
System.out.println(a == b);  // true — primitives: value comparison
// ✅ Wrapper Integer: == only reliable for -128 to 127 (cache range)
System.out.println(i3 == i4);      // false (outside cache — new objects!)
System.out.println(i3.equals(i4)); // true  ✅ always use .equals() for wrappers

blocks.title: ⚠️ == vs .equals() — The Most Common Java Bug
blocks.text: For objects (String, Integer, custom classes), == compares memory references, not content. Always use .equals() for content comparison. For primitives (int, char, double, boolean), use ==. For wrapper types (Integer, Double, etc.), use .equals(). For null checks, use == null (not .equals() — that throws NullPointerException). Summary: primitives → ==, objects → .equals(), null → == null.

Logical operators combine or invert boolean expressions and always return a boolean result. Java provides three logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), and ! (NOT). The AND and OR operators use short-circuit evaluation — one of the most important Java evaluation behaviors to understand for writing safe, efficient code.

items.title: && (Logical AND) — Short-Circuit
items.text: Returns true only if BOTH operands are true. Short-circuits: if the left operand is false, the right operand is never evaluated. Use this for safe null checks: if (obj != null && obj.getValue() > 0) — if obj is null, obj.getValue() is never called. Prevents NullPointerException. Both operands MUST be boolean.

items.title: || (Logical OR) — Short-Circuit
items.text: Returns true if AT LEAST ONE operand is true. Short-circuits: if the left operand is true, the right operand is never evaluated. Use for default value patterns: if (name != null || (name = getDefault()) != null). The right side only runs when needed. Performance tip: put the more likely true condition on the left for OR, and the more likely false condition on the left for AND.

items.title: & and | (Non-Short-Circuit)
items.text: The bitwise & and | operators, when used with boolean operands, behave like && and || but WITHOUT short-circuit evaluation — BOTH sides are always evaluated. Rarely used for logical operations. Use case: when the right-side expression MUST be evaluated for its side effects (e.g., incrementing a counter). In general, prefer && and || for boolean logic.

blocks.label: LogicalOperators.java
lines: System.out.println(a && b);  // false — AND: both must be true
System.out.println(a || b);  // true  — OR: at least one true
if (str != null && str.length() > 0) {  // str.length() never called if str == null
System.out.println("String is null or empty"); // Safe!
// ✅ Short-circuit OR — right side only runs if left is false
System.out.println(count);  // 1 — right side WAS evaluated (left was false)
System.out.println(count2); // 1 — right side NOT evaluated (left was true, short-circuit!)
// ✅ De Morgan's Laws — useful for simplifying conditions

blocks.text: Assignment operators assign values to variables. The basic assignment operator is =. Java also provides compound assignment operators that combine an arithmetic or bitwise operation with assignment in a single step. For example, x += 5 is shorthand for x = x + 5. Compound operators are more concise and also perform an implicit narrowing cast — an important detail when working with byte and short types.

lines: // ✅ Implicit narrowing cast with compound assignment
// b = b + 5;    // ❌ Compile error: int cannot be converted to byte
b += 5;          // ✅ Works! Compound += includes implicit (byte) cast
a = c = d = 100;  // All assigned 100 — right to left
// ✅ Assignment is itself an expression (returns assigned value)
if ((val = getValue()) > 0) {  // Assigns AND checks in one step

blocks.text: Unary operators operate on a single operand. Java provides five unary operators: + (unary plus), - (unary minus/negation), ++ (increment), -- (decrement), and ! (logical NOT). The increment and decrement operators have two forms — prefix (++x) and postfix (x++) — which behave differently inside expressions.

items.title: Prefix vs Postfix Increment/Decrement
items.text: Prefix (++x or --x): modifies the variable FIRST, then returns the NEW value. Postfix (x++ or x--): returns the CURRENT (original) value first, THEN modifies the variable. As a standalone statement (e.g., i++ on its own line), both are identical. The difference only matters when the expression value is used — inside assignments, method calls, array indexing, or larger expressions.

items.title: Increment Inside Expressions — Be Careful
items.text: Avoid using ++ or -- inside complex expressions — the result is hard to predict and varies by evaluation order. Example: int x = 5; int y = x++ + ++x; — y = 12 (tricky!). Best practice: use increment operators only as standalone statements (i++ on its own line), not embedded inside larger expressions. This prevents confusion and makes intent clear.

blocks.label: UnaryOperators.java
lines: System.out.println(+a);   // 5  — unary plus (no change for positive)
// ✅ Prefix vs Postfix — the key difference
System.out.println(x++);  // 10 — returns CURRENT value, THEN increments
System.out.println(++y);  // 11 — increments FIRST, then returns NEW value
// ✅ Postfix in a loop (most common use)
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {  // i++ is fine here as standalone
int result = ++n * 2;  // n becomes 6 first, then 6 * 2 = 12
// ⚠️ Even trickier — avoid this in real code
int tricky = m++ + ++m;  // m++ returns 5 (m→6), ++m returns 7 (m→7): 5+7=12
System.out.println(tricky); // 12 — but this style is unreadable, avoid it!

blocks.text: Bitwise operators operate directly on the binary representation (individual bits) of integer types (int, long, byte, short). They are used in low-level programming, performance-sensitive code, permission systems, flags, encryption, and embedded systems. Java provides four bitwise operators: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), and ~ (bitwise complement/NOT).

items.title: & (Bitwise AND)
items.text: Sets a bit to 1 only if BOTH corresponding bits are 1. Otherwise 0. Example: 12 & 10 = 8 (1100 & 1010 = 1000). Common use: masking (isolating specific bits). Check if a bit is set: if ((flags & 0x01) != 0). Also used to check even/odd: n & 1 == 0 means even (faster than n % 2).

items.title: | (Bitwise OR)
items.text: Sets a bit to 1 if EITHER corresponding bit is 1. Example: 12 | 10 = 14 (1100 | 1010 = 1110). Common use: setting specific bits (flags). Turn on a bit: flags |= 0x04. Used in permission systems to grant rights: permissions |= READ_PERMISSION.

items.title: ^ (Bitwise XOR) and ~ (Complement)
items.text: XOR (^): sets bit to 1 if bits DIFFER, 0 if same. 12 ^ 10 = 6 (1100 ^ 1010 = 0110). Used to toggle bits and in encryption/hashing. ~ (complement): inverts ALL bits. ~5 = -6 (in two's complement). Rule: ~n = -(n+1). Use for toggling flags: flags ^= 0x02.

blocks.label: BitwiseOperators.java
lines: // ✅ Real-world: permission flags using bitwise operators
// ✅ Permission system using bitwise OR to grant, AND to check
System.out.println("Read after toggle: " + ((userPermissions & READ) != 0)); // false (was true)
// ✅ Fast even/odd check with bitwise AND

blocks.text: Shift operators move the bits of an integer value left or right by a specified number of positions. Java provides three shift operators: << (left shift), >> (signed/arithmetic right shift), and >>> (unsigned/logical right shift). Shift operators are commonly used in performance optimization (powers of 2), data packing, hashing algorithms, and low-level system code.

items.title: << (Left Shift)
items.text: Shifts bits to the left, filling vacated positions on the right with 0s. Each left shift by 1 is equivalent to multiplying by 2. n << k = n * 2^k. Example: 5 << 1 = 10, 5 << 2 = 20. Bits shifted beyond the 32/64 bit boundary are lost. Commonly used for fast multiplication by powers of 2 and bit packing.

items.title: >> (Signed Right Shift)
items.text: Shifts bits to the right, filling vacated positions on the left with the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative). Preserves the sign. Each right shift by 1 is equivalent to integer division by 2 (floor for negatives). n >> k = n / 2^k. Example: 20 >> 1 = 10, -20 >> 1 = -10. Safe for all signed integers.

items.title: >>> (Unsigned Right Shift)
items.text: Shifts bits to the right, ALWAYS filling vacated positions with 0 — regardless of sign. Does not preserve sign bit. For positive numbers, same as >>. For negative numbers, result is a large positive number. Used in hashing (HashMap uses >>> 16 for hash spreading) and graphics/color manipulation where you want raw bit manipulation without sign extension.

blocks.label: ShiftOperators.java
lines: // ✅ Left shift — multiply by power of 2
// ✅ Signed right shift — divide by power of 2
// ✅ Unsigned right shift — sign bit filled with 0
// ✅ Real-world: fast power of 2 check using bit manipulation
System.out.println(num + " is power of 2: " + isPowerOfTwo); // true
int spread = hash ^ (hash >>> 16);  // XOR with upper 16 bits
// ✅ Extract RGB color components from packed int
System.out.printf("A=%d R=%d G=%d B=%d%n", alpha, red, green, blue);

blocks.text: The ternary operator (?:) is Java's only operator that takes three operands. It provides a compact way to write a simple if-else expression in a single line. Syntax: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. The condition must evaluate to a boolean, and both branches must return compatible types. The ternary operator is an expression (returns a value) unlike an if-else statement — so it can be used directly in assignments, method arguments, and string concatenation.

blocks.label: TernaryOperator.java
lines: // ✅ Chained ternary (use sparingly — readability drops fast)
// ⚠️ Bad practice: ternary with side effects — avoid
// int x = (count++ > 0) ? count++ : count--;  // Confusing — use if-else instead

blocks.title: 💡 When to Use Ternary vs if-else
blocks.text: Use ternary for: (1) Simple value selection — int max = a > b ? a : b. (2) Inline expressions — method arguments, string concatenation. (3) Null defaults — String val = str != null ? str : 'default'. Avoid ternary for: (1) Complex conditions needing explanation. (2) Nested ternaries beyond 2 levels — readability collapses. (3) Expressions with side effects. Rule of thumb: if you can read it aloud in one breath, ternary is fine. Otherwise, use if-else.

The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class, subclass, or interface — returning a boolean. It is commonly used before downcasting to prevent ClassCastException. Java 16 introduced pattern matching for instanceof, which combines the check and cast in a single step — eliminating boilerplate and improving readability.

blocks.label: InstanceofOperator.java
lines: System.out.println(a1 instanceof Animal); // true  — Dog IS-A Animal
System.out.println(a1 instanceof Dog);    // true  — actual type is Dog
System.out.println(a1 instanceof Cat);    // false — Dog is NOT a Cat
System.out.println(a3 instanceof Animal); // false — null is never instanceof anything
Dog d = (Dog) a1;   // Safe cast after instanceof check
// ✅ Java 16+ Pattern Matching — check AND cast in one step
if (a1 instanceof Dog dog) {   // 'dog' is automatically cast and in scope
// ✅ Pattern matching in a loop (polymorphic processing)
Animal[] animals = { new Dog(), new Cat(), new Dog() };

blocks.text: Operator precedence determines which operator is evaluated first when multiple operators appear in the same expression. Operators with higher precedence bind more tightly to their operands. When operators have equal precedence, associativity determines direction: most operators are left-to-right, but assignment and unary are right-to-left. Best practice: always use parentheses to make intent explicit instead of relying on precedence rules.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns represent common misuses of operators in professional Java code. Each one reduces readability, introduces bugs, or signals misunderstanding of the language.

items.title: Using == for Object Equality
items.text: Using == to compare Strings, Integers, or custom objects checks reference identity, not value. String a = new String('x'); String b = new String('x'); a == b is false. Always use .equals() for objects. For null-safe comparison, use Objects.equals(a, b) which handles null without NullPointerException. This is the single most common Java bug in beginner code.

items.title: Deeply Nested Ternary Chains
items.text: Chaining more than 2 levels of ternary operators creates code that is nearly impossible to read, debug, or modify. Replace with a clear if-else-if ladder or a switch expression. The ternary operator exists for simple one-liners — using it as a replacement for complex conditional logic is an anti-pattern that most code review teams will reject.

items.title: Relying on Implicit Operator Precedence
items.text: Writing expressions like 'a + b > c && d || e' without parentheses forces every reader to mentally recall the precedence table. This is error-prone and slows code review. Always use parentheses to make complex expressions unambiguous: '((a + b) > c) && (d || e)'. Parentheses are free — unambiguous code is priceless.

items.title: Increment Operators in Complex Expressions
items.text: Embedding ++ or -- inside larger expressions — array[i++] = j-- or method(i++, ++j) — creates subtle evaluation-order bugs and reduces readability. Use increment operators as standalone statements only (i++ or ++i on their own line). Let the next line use the updated value. This is the style enforced by most major Java style guides and static analysis tools.

items.title: Ignoring Integer Overflow
items.text: Java silently wraps integer values on overflow without throwing any exception. int x = Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 = -2147483648 — no warning, no error. In financial calculations, counters, or array index arithmetic, this causes catastrophic silent bugs. Use long for large values, Math.addExact() / multiplyExact() for overflow detection, or BigInteger for arbitrary precision.

items.title: Using Bitwise Operators for Boolean Logic
items.text: Using & and | instead of && and || for boolean conditions disables short-circuit evaluation. This causes NullPointerException when the right side is null-sensitive: if (obj != null & obj.method() > 0) — obj.method() is ALWAYS called, even when obj is null. Always use && and || for boolean logic. Reserve & and | for intentional non-short-circuit scenarios (rare) or actual bitwise operations on integers.

sections.title: Java Operators Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java developer interviews at all levels. Mastering these will solidify your understanding of Java operators.

items.q: Q1. What are the types of operators in Java?
items.a: Java has 8 categories of operators: (1) Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %) — math operations. (2) Relational (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=) — comparison, returns boolean. (3) Logical (&&, ||, !) — boolean expression combination. (4) Assignment (=, +=, -=, etc.) — assign values. (5) Unary (++, --, +, -, !) — single operand operations. (6) Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~) — bit-level operations on integers. (7) Shift (<<, >>, >>>) — bit shifting. (8) Ternary (?:) — compact conditional expression. Additionally, instanceof checks object type. By operand count: unary (1 operand), binary (2 operands), ternary (3 operands — Java's only one).

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
items.a: == compares references (memory addresses) for objects and actual values for primitives. .equals() compares content/value of objects. For primitives (int, double, char, boolean): use ==. For objects (String, Integer, custom classes): use .equals() for content comparison. Common trap: Integer i1 = 200; Integer i2 = 200; i1 == i2 is false (outside the Integer cache range -128 to 127). i1.equals(i2) is true. For null-safe comparison, use Objects.equals(a, b) instead of a.equals(b) — the latter throws NPE if a is null.

items.q: Q3. What is short-circuit evaluation? How does it differ from & and |?
items.a: Short-circuit evaluation means Java stops evaluating a logical expression as soon as the result is determined. && (short-circuit AND): if left is false, right is never evaluated. || (short-circuit OR): if left is true, right is never evaluated. & and | (non-short-circuit): BOTH sides are ALWAYS evaluated, regardless of the left side result. Key difference: with &&, 'if (obj != null && obj.method() > 0)' is safe — obj.method() is never called when obj is null. With &, obj.method() IS called even when obj is null → NullPointerException. Use && and || for boolean logic; reserve & and | for bitwise operations.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between prefix (++x) and postfix (x++) increment?
items.a: Prefix (++x): increments first, then returns the new value. Postfix (x++): returns the current value first, then increments. Example: int x = 5; int a = ++x; — a = 6, x = 6. int y = 5; int b = y++; — b = 5, y = 6. As a standalone statement (i++ on its own line), both are functionally identical. The difference ONLY matters when the result of the expression is used — inside assignments, method arguments, array indexes, etc. Best practice: use increment operators only as standalone statements to avoid confusion.

items.q: Q5. What is operator precedence? What is the order for +, *, >, && and ||?
items.a: Operator precedence determines which operator is evaluated first in an expression with multiple operators. From highest to lowest among these: * (multiplicative) > + (additive) > > (relational) > && (logical AND) > || (logical OR). So 'a + b * c > d && e || f' evaluates as: (a + (b*c)) > d) && e) || f. Assignment operators have the lowest precedence (right-to-left). Unary and postfix have the highest. Parentheses always override precedence. Best practice: always use parentheses in complex expressions to make intent explicit — never rely on memorizing precedence in production code.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between >> and >>> in Java?
items.a: Both shift bits right. >> (signed/arithmetic right shift): fills vacated bits on the left with the sign bit — 0 for positive, 1 for negative. Preserves sign: -64 >> 2 = -16. >>> (unsigned/logical right shift): always fills vacated bits with 0, regardless of sign. Does not preserve sign: -64 >>> 2 = a large positive number. For positive numbers, >> and >>> behave identically. Use >> when sign preservation is needed (equivalent to integer division by power of 2 for positive numbers). Use >>> for raw bit manipulation, color channel extraction, or hashing (Java's HashMap uses >>> 16 for hash spreading).

items.q: Q7. What happens when you use the + operator with String and int values?
items.a: The + operator is overloaded: for numeric types it performs addition; when one operand is a String, it performs concatenation (converts the other operand to String). Evaluation is left-to-right. Critical examples: 1 + 2 + '3' = '33' (1+2=3, then 3+'3'='33'). '1' + 2 + 3 = '123' ('1'+2='12', then '12'+3='123'). '1' + (2 + 3) = '15' (parentheses: 2+3=5, then '1'+5='15'). This left-to-right evaluation and the implicit toString conversion of non-String operands is a very common source of subtle bugs. Always use parentheses when mixing arithmetic and string concatenation.

items.q: Q8. What is the result of -7 % 3 in Java? How do you get a always-positive modulus?
items.a: In Java, the % operator follows the rule: result takes the sign of the dividend (left operand). So -7 % 3 = -1 (not 2). Similarly, 7 % -3 = 1. To get a mathematically correct always-positive modulus (matching mathematical convention), use Math.floorMod(a, b): Math.floorMod(-7, 3) = 2. This is useful for circular indexing, clock arithmetic, or wrapping array indexes. The difference: % is 'remainder' (Java/C), Math.floorMod is 'modulo' (mathematical). For non-negative dividends, both give the same result.

items.q: Q9. What is the ternary operator? When should you use it vs if-else?
items.a: The ternary operator (?:) is Java's only three-operand operator: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. It is an expression (returns a value) unlike if-else (a statement). Use ternary for: (1) simple value selection — int max = a > b ? a : b. (2) Null default — String s = val != null ? val : 'default'. (3) Inline use in method arguments or string concatenation. Avoid ternary for: (1) Complex conditions — reduces readability. (2) Nested ternaries beyond 2 levels — use if-else-if or switch. (3) Operations with side effects. Rule: if you can read the ternary naturally in one breath, it's fine. Otherwise, the if-else is clearer.

items.q: Q10. What does the instanceof operator do in Java 16+ pattern matching?
items.a: Traditional instanceof: 'if (obj instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) obj; d.fetch(); }' — requires a separate explicit cast after the check. Java 16 pattern matching: 'if (obj instanceof Dog dog) { dog.fetch(); }' — combines the instanceof check AND the cast in a single step. The variable 'dog' is automatically cast and scoped within the if block. Benefits: (1) No explicit cast needed. (2) No ClassCastException risk — cast only happens after the check. (3) Less boilerplate. (4) The pattern variable is in scope only where the type is guaranteed. Null is never instanceof anything — null instanceof Dog is always false, so no null check is needed before instanceof.

blocks.text: Challenge yourself with these practice questions. Attempt each independently before reading the answer — active recall is proven to be 2–3x more effective than passive reading.

This is the classic integer-division-vs-float-division question. Always cast to double when you need decimal precision from integer operands.

Output: false, true, true. (1) s1 == s2: false — both are new String() objects with different references even though content is same. == compares references for objects. (2) s3 == s4: true — string literals are stored in the String pool, so 'hello' and 'hello' refer to the same pool object. (3) s1.equals(s2): true — .equals() compares content. Key lesson: never use == for String comparison in production code. Always use .equals().

Output: 5, 6, 7, 7. (1) x++ returns current value (5), THEN increments x to 6. (2) x is now 6. (3) ++x increments x to 7 FIRST, then returns 7. (4) x is still 7. This demonstrates the fundamental difference between postfix (return current, then modify) and prefix (modify first, then return new value).

Output: '33', '123', '15', '6!'. (1) 1+2=3 (int), then 3+'3'='33' (concat). (2) '1'+2='12' (concat), then '12'+3='123' (concat). (3) (2+3)=5 (int in parens), then '1'+5='15' (concat). (4) 1+2=3, 3+3=6 (all int, no String yet), then 6+'!'='6!' (concat). Evaluation is strictly left-to-right — as soon as a String operand appears on the left, subsequent + operations become concatenation.

Output: 2, 1. (1) For ||: left side 'count++ > 0' → count=0 is NOT > 0 (false), so count becomes 1 (postfix), but the result is false. Since left is false, || cannot short-circuit, so right side '++count > 0' IS evaluated: count becomes 2, returns true. count = 2. (2) For &&: left side 'count2++ > 0' → count2=0 is NOT > 0 (false), count2 becomes 1. Since left is false, && short-circuits and right side is NEVER evaluated. count2 stays at 1. This demonstrates that || short-circuits when left is TRUE, and && short-circuits when left is FALSE.

Ternary version: String result = marks >= 60 ? 'Pass' : 'Fail'; — clean, readable, and concise. Yes, ternary is appropriate here because: (1) it's a simple binary choice, (2) no side effects, (3) result is assigned directly. The ternary is not always better: if the condition were complex, had multiple branches, or involved statements (not just expressions), the if-else would be clearer. Rule: ternary is ideal for simple conditional value assignment; if-else is better for complex logic or multiple outcomes.

Output: 8, 14, 6, -11. (1) a & b: 1010 & 1100 = 1000 = 8 — AND: both bits must be 1. (2) a | b: 1010 | 1100 = 1110 = 14 — OR: either bit can be 1. (3) a ^ b: 1010 ^ 1100 = 0110 = 6 — XOR: bits must DIFFER. (4) ~a: inverts ALL bits of 10 (00...01010) → 11...10101 = -11 in two's complement. Rule for ~: ~n = -(n+1). So ~10 = -11.

Line 2 does NOT compile: 'b + 5' produces an int (Java widens to int for arithmetic), and int cannot be assigned to byte without explicit cast. Compile error: 'possible lossy conversion from int to byte'. Line 3 compiles and works: the compound += operator includes an implicit narrowing cast to byte. Fix: b = (byte)(b + 5); for line 2. After the fix (or skipping line 2): b += 5 makes b = 20. Output: 20. This demonstrates the important difference between plain assignment (no implicit cast) and compound assignment (implicit narrowing cast included).

sections.title: Conclusion — Operators: The Building Blocks of Every Java Expression

blocks.text: Operators are the foundation of every expression in Java. From the simplest int sum = a + b to complex business logic involving short-circuit null guards, bitwise permission flags, and ternary value selection — operators are present in every line of meaningful Java code. Understanding them deeply separates functional code from professional code.

The most important takeaways: always use .equals() for object comparison (never ==), leverage short-circuit evaluation (&& and ||) for null safety, use parentheses to make operator precedence explicit, avoid increment operators inside complex expressions, and never ignore integer overflow in production arithmetic. These are the habits that distinguish senior Java developers.

items.q: What are operators in Java?
items.a: Operators in Java are special symbols or keywords that perform operations on one or more operands and produce a result. Java provides 8 categories: Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), Relational (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=), Logical (&&, ||, !), Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~), Shift (<<, >>, >>>), Assignment (=, +=, etc.), Unary (++, --, !, +, -), and Ternary (?:). Additionally, instanceof checks object type. By operand count: unary operators take 1 operand, binary take 2, and the ternary takes 3.

items.q: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
items.a: == compares references (memory addresses) for objects and actual values for primitives. .equals() compares the actual content of objects. For primitives, use ==. For objects like String, Integer, or custom classes, always use .equals(). Common trap: new String('hello') == new String('hello') is false even though content is identical. Use Objects.equals(a, b) for null-safe object comparison. This is the most common Java bug in beginner code.

items.q: What is short-circuit evaluation in Java?
items.a: Short-circuit evaluation means Java stops evaluating a logical expression as soon as the result is certain. && (AND): if left is false, right is never evaluated. || (OR): if left is true, right is never evaluated. This enables safe null checks: if (obj != null && obj.getValue() > 0) — obj.getValue() is never called when obj is null. The non-short-circuit versions & and | always evaluate both sides — use them only when both sides must be evaluated for their side effects.

items.q: What is operator precedence in Java?
items.a: Operator precedence determines the order of evaluation when multiple operators appear in one expression. Higher precedence means evaluated first. From highest to lowest (simplified): postfix (x++) → unary (-x, ++x) → multiplicative (*, /, %) → additive (+, -) → shift (<< >>) → relational (< > instanceof) → equality (== !=) → bitwise AND (&) → bitwise XOR (^) → bitwise OR (|) → logical AND (&&) → logical OR (||) → ternary (?:) → assignment (=, +=, etc.). Best practice: always use parentheses in complex expressions rather than relying on precedence.

items.q: What is the difference between prefix and postfix increment operators?
items.a: Prefix (++x): increments the variable FIRST, then returns the new value. Postfix (x++): returns the current (original) value FIRST, then increments. Example: int x = 5; int a = ++x → a=6, x=6. int y = 5; int b = y++ → b=5, y=6. As a standalone statement (i++ on its own line), both are identical. The difference only matters when the expression value is used in a larger context — inside assignments, method arguments, or expressions.
